summary: For learners aged 9–11: birds are living theropod dinosaurs, a conclusion each child should read off anatomy rather than accept as a slogan. The central activity places a small feathered theropod, Archaeopteryx, and a modern bird side by side so learners find shared features themselves — wishbone (furcula), hollow (pneumatic) bones, three main forward-pointing toes, S-curved neck, and feathers — then examine Archaeopteryx as a mosaic combining modern-bird-like traits (flight feathers, feathered wings) with traits typical of earlier non-avian theropods (teeth, clawed fingers, long bony tail). The goal is for learners to conclude, with evidence, that birds are classified inside theropod dinosaurs and that only the non-avian dinosaurs died out. Links to UK DfE Y6 Evolution & inheritance (fossils as evidence of past life) and NGSS 3-LS4-1, MS-LS4-1/MS-LS4-2 (anatomical similarity and fossils as evidence of evolutionary relationships).
misconceptions: 'Birds are descended FROM dinosaurs but are not themselves dinosaurs' — in fact birds ARE dinosaurs (a surviving theropod lineage).
'Feathers mean it was a bird' — many non-avian dinosaurs had feathers; feathers evolved before flight.
'Archaeopteryx is the single ancestor of all birds / the missing link' — it is one transitional form illustrating the pattern, not a direct sole ancestor.
'All dinosaurs went extinct' — avian dinosaurs survived and are all around us.
'Pterosaurs (flying reptiles) were dinosaurs / bird ancestors' — they are neither; bird flight arose within theropods.

activities.title: Find the shared bones: raptor, Archaeopteryx, pigeon
steps: Examine three images or models side by side: a small feathered raptor (left), Archaeopteryx (middle), and a modern pigeon (right).
Locate the pigeon's wishbone (furcula), then find and point to the matching fused collarbone in the raptor and Archaeopteryx (its shape varies, from V- or U-shaped to boomerang-shaped).
Repeat for hollow (pneumatic) bones and the three main forward-pointing toes, naming each shared feature aloud or in writing before being told the conclusion.
Record a list of at least two skeletal features that a pigeon and a theropod such as Velociraptor or T. rex share.
Only after collecting the evidence, state in your own words why birds can be called living dinosaurs.
activities.insight: Birds and theropod dinosaurs share the same body parts (wishbone, hollow bones, three-toed feet), which is evidence that birds belong inside the theropod dinosaur group — a conclusion the learner reaches feature by feature rather than being told.

activities.title: Archaeopteryx as a mosaic
steps: Look closely at a reconstruction of Archaeopteryx (about 150 million years old, Late Jurassic).
Sort its features into two columns: traits like modern birds (flight feathers, feathered wings) and traits like earlier non-avian theropods (teeth, clawed fingers, long bony tail).
Explain in a sentence or two why a fossil that shows both sets of traits at once is called a 'transitional' fossil.
Discuss why such a creature is expected evidence for evolution, not a strange exception.
activities.insight: Transitional forms like Archaeopteryx are real and expected: a single animal can carry a mixture of older features seen in non-avian theropods and newer features seen in modern birds, documenting change over time.

activities.title: Feathers before flight
steps: Study an image of a feathered non-avian dinosaur that could NOT fly (for example a small flightless feathered theropod among the exceptionally preserved specimens from the Liaoning deposits in China), showing feather impressions around a clearly non-bird skeleton.
Note the evidence scientists use to infer that this animal could not fly (for example short arms and simple, fluffy rather than flight-shaped feathers), yet see that it had feathers anyway.
Suggest what feathers might have been useful for before flight (for example insulation/warmth or display).
Write a sentence explaining why 'feathers mean it was a bird' is not correct.
activities.insight: Feathers evolved before flight and were present on many non-avian dinosaurs, so feathers are not unique to birds; they were later co-opted for flight.

activities.title: Which dinosaurs survived? (defend the claim)
steps: Respond to a friend who says: 'Birds can't be related to dinosaurs — dinosaurs were huge scaly reptiles and they all died out, but birds are small and have feathers.'
Write what you would say back, citing at least one transitional or feathered fossil and at least two shared skeletal features.
State clearly which dinosaurs went extinct and which survived: the non-avian dinosaurs died out, while one lineage lives on as birds.
Finish with a formal statement: birds are classified inside the theropod dinosaurs, so the dinosaurs never fully died out.
activities.insight: Birds are a surviving theropod lineage: only the non-avian dinosaurs became extinct, and the bird–dinosaur link is supported by fossils and shared anatomy, not just asserted.

checkQuestion: Your friend says: 'Birds can't be related to dinosaurs — dinosaurs were huge scaly reptiles and they all died out, but birds are small and have feathers.' What would you say back, and what evidence would you use?
checkAnswer: Birds evolved from small feathered theropod dinosaurs and are themselves living dinosaurs — so not all dinosaurs died out. Evidence: Archaeopteryx and Chinese feathered-dinosaur fossils show feathers on dinosaurs that couldn't fly; birds share skeletal features with theropods (hollow bones, a wishbone, three-toed feet). Feathers existed before flight.
